common_name: Salanova Lettuce (Compact Cut-and-Come-Again Salad Lettuce Series)

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Salanova is a breeding breakthrough lettuce series designed so that a single head, cut once at the base, falls apart into dozens of perfectly bite-sized, ready-to-eat baby leaves, dramatically speeding harvest compared to picking individual leaves by hand.

directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Salanova is a lettuce series bred specifically to solve the labor problem of harvesting baby salad greens leaf by leaf: each Salanova head grows as a tight rosette of dozens of small, uniform, bite-sized leaves attached at a single central core, so cutting the plant once at the base instantly yields a full bowl of ready-to-eat, pre-washed-looking salad leaves rather than a single lettuce head that needs chopping. It comes in multiple types — butterhead, oakleaf, and incised (frilly) forms in both green and red — allowing gardeners to plant a mix for varied color and texture in a single cutting. Because the leaves are already small, individual heads can be spaced fairly closely for high-density production, and successive sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply coming through the cool season. It bolts readily in summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best results in zone 9, and provide afternoon shade for any late-spring or early-fall plantings that overlap with warm weather.

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Adriana is a Little Gem-type miniature romaine bred for fast maturity and heat tolerance, producing dense, sweet, crunchy heads well suited to close spacing and succession planting.

directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Adriana is a miniature romaine lettuce in the Little Gem tradition, producing small, dense, upright heads with crisp outer leaves and a sweet, tender heart, but bred for notably faster maturity and better heat tolerance than older Little Gem strains, letting gardeners push both the early spring and late fall ends of the lettuce season a bit further. Its compact size makes it well suited to intensive spacing and container growing, and the whole small heads work perfectly as individual salad or Caesar-salad portions without needing to be cut down for a mixed bowl. Harvest the whole head once it feels firm and dense at the base, or begin picking outer leaves earlier for a cut-and-come-again approach. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to delay bolting as temperatures rise.

common_name: Outredgeous Lettuce (Deep Red Romaine, First Lettuce Grown in Space)

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Outredgeous is a deep burgundy-red romaine lettuce famous as the first crop grown and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station, and a reliable, richly colored performer in the home garden.

directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Outredgeous is an open-pollinated romaine lettuce selected for intensely dark red-burgundy outer leaves that shade to green toward the crisp, upright heart, giving each head striking two-tone color as well as classic romaine crunch and mild, sweet flavor. It gained widespread recognition in 2015 as the first food crop grown, harvested, and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station as part of NASA's Veggie experiment, chosen partly for its rich anthocyanin pigmentation and reliable performance. In the home garden it is simply a vigorous, dependable, good-flavored red romaine, harvested either as whole heads once firm or as individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again approach. It bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best quality in zone 9, providing afternoon shade for plantings that overlap with warm weather.

common_name: Sea of Red Lettuce (Deep Red Frilly Oakleaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Sea of Red is a deeply colored, frilly-leaved oakleaf lettuce that holds its intense burgundy-red color and resists bolting and bitterness longer than many other red lettuce varieties, making it a reliable performer through a wider harvest window.

directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Sea of Red is an oakleaf-type lettuce prized for deeply lobed, ruffled, deep burgundy-red leaves that stay glossy and appetizing-looking even as outer leaves are repeatedly harvested, making it a favorite for cut-and-come-again baby leaf production as well as full-head harvest. It holds its rich color and resists premature bolting and the bitterness that develops in many red lettuces once temperatures climb, giving it a somewhat longer productive window than more heat-sensitive varieties, though it still performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons in zone 9. Harvest outer leaves as needed for continuous production, or cut the whole loose head at once for a single larger harvest. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings to further delay bolting as the weather warms.

common_name: New Red Fire Lettuce (Improved Heat-Tolerant Red Leaf Lettuce)

planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; New Red Fire is an improved loose-leaf red lettuce bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf varieties, making it one of the more reliable red lettuces for a longer Gulf South spring and fall season.

directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. New Red Fire is a loose-leaf lettuce bearing large, ruffled, deep red-tinged leaves over a green base, an improved selection bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf lettuce varieties, which makes it noticeably more forgiving for gardeners in warm climates trying to stretch the lettuce season into early summer or start it earlier in late winter. Because it is a loose-leaf type, it never forms a tight head, and outer leaves can be harvested continuously while the center keeps producing new growth, extending the useful harvest window from a single planting. Flavor is mild and pleasant even as leaves size up, without the pronounced bitterness that develops quickly in less heat-tolerant lettuce under stress. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to further delay bolting as temperatures climb.
